at dividere.explanation: "At dividere" means "to divide" in math. To share something between people, say "at dele" (to share).

sentence.da: Du skal **dividere** tolv med tre.
sentence.en: You have to divide twelve by three.

at dokumentere.explanation: "At dokumentere" means "to document", to show with papers, photos or numbers that something is true or has happened.

sentence.da: Du skal **dokumentere** dine udgifter med kvitteringer.
sentence.en: You must document your expenses with receipts.

at dominere.explanation: "At dominere" means "to dominate", to be the strongest or most noticeable part of something. A person can do it in a conversation: "Han dominerer samtalen" (He dominates the conversation). A color can do it too: "Blå dominerer billedet" (Blue dominates the picture).

sentence.da: Det bedste hold kan **dominere** kampen fra første minut.
sentence.en: The best team can dominate the match from the first minute.

at donere.explanation: "At donere" means "to donate", to give money, things, blood or organs without getting anything in return. To name the person or group that receives the gift, add "til" (to): "Jeg donerer penge til Røde Kors" (I donate money to the Red Cross).

sentence.da: Mange vil gerne **donere** blod, fordi det kan redde liv.
sentence.en: Many people want to donate blood because it can save lives.

at downloade.explanation: "At downloade" means "to download", to copy something from the internet onto your own device.

sentence.da: Jeg vil **downloade** en film til min telefon.
sentence.en: I want to download a movie to my phone.

at drage.explanation: "At drage" means "to draw" in set phrases such as "at drage en konklusion" (to draw a conclusion). It also means "to go" when someone sets out on a journey, but in an old-fashioned, storybook way: "Han drog ud i verden" (He set out into the world). For an ordinary trip, people say "at tage af sted" (to leave).

sentence.da: Efter testen kan vi **drage** en klar konklusion.
sentence.en: After the test, we can draw a clear conclusion.

at dreje.explanation: "At dreje" means "to turn". To say what something is about, use "at dreje sig om" (to be about): "Det drejer sig om penge" (It is about money).

sentence.da: Du skal **dreje** til venstre ved banken.
sentence.en: You have to turn left at the bank.

at drikke.explanation: "At drikke" means "to drink", for any liquid such as water, coffee and beer. "Jeg drikker ikke" (I do not drink) usually means you do not drink alcohol.

sentence.da: Jeg vil **drikke** et glas vand.
sentence.en: I want to drink a glass of water.

at drille.explanation: "At drille" means "to tease", usually in a playful way. Teasing that hurts is closer to "at mobbe" (to bully).

sentence.da: Min bror elsker at **drille** mig.
sentence.en: My brother loves to tease me.

at drive.explanation: "At drive" means "to run" a business: "at drive en butik" (to run a shop). It also means "to drift", to be carried along by wind or water: "Skyerne driver hen over himlen" (The clouds drift across the sky).

sentence.da: Hun vil **drive** sin egen café på havnen.
sentence.en: She wants to run her own cafe at the harbor.

at droppe.explanation: "At droppe" means "to drop" a plan or "to skip" something: "Vi dropper planen" (We are dropping the plan), "Jeg dropper morgenmaden" (I am skipping breakfast).

sentence.da: Jeg vil **droppe** sukker i min kaffe.
sentence.en: I want to skip sugar in my coffee.

at drukne.explanation: "At drukne" means "to drown", to die by being under water and not being able to breathe.

sentence.da: Man kan **drukne** i dybt vand.
sentence.en: You can drown in deep water.

at dryppe.explanation: "At dryppe" means "to drip", to fall in single drops, like water from a roof after rain. It also means to put drops on something: "at dryppe citron på fisken" (to drip lemon on the fish).

sentence.da: Hanen i køkkenet kan **dryppe** hele natten.
sentence.en: The tap in the kitchen can drip all night.

at drysse.explanation: "At drysse" means "to sprinkle", to let small pieces fall lightly over something. For light snow or rain, Danes say "Det drysser" (It is sprinkling).

sentence.da: Man kan **drysse** kanel over risengrød.
sentence.en: You can sprinkle cinnamon over rice pudding.

at dræbe.explanation: "At dræbe" means "to kill". To say someone was killed, Danish uses "blev" (was) with "dræbt" (killed): "Han blev dræbt" (He was killed).

sentence.da: Ræven kan **dræbe** en høne.
sentence.en: The fox can kill a hen.

at drøfte.explanation: "At drøfte" means "to discuss", to talk something through carefully, for example in a meeting. It needs no small word before what you discuss: "Vi drøfter budgettet" (We are discussing the budget). "At tale om" (to talk about) needs "om" (about): "Vi taler om budgettet" (We are talking about the budget).

sentence.da: Bestyrelsen skal **drøfte** forslaget på næste møde.
sentence.en: The board must discuss the proposal at the next meeting.

at drømme.explanation: "At drømme" means "to dream", both asleep and awake, and it takes "om" (about): "Jeg drømte om dig" (I dreamed about you).

sentence.da: Jeg vil sove og **drømme** hele natten.
sentence.en: I want to sleep and dream all night.

at dufte.explanation: "At dufte" means "to smell nice". "At lugte" (to smell) can also mean a bad smell: "Det lugter af fisk" (It smells like fish).

sentence.da: Det plejer at **dufte** dejligt her.
sentence.en: It usually smells lovely here.

at duge.explanation: "At duge" means "to be any good", to be good enough for a purpose. The verb is mostly used in a negative sentence: "Det duer ikke" (That will not do). "Duer" is also the plural of "en due" (a dove). You can tell which meaning is used from the context of the sentence.

forms.en: I have been any good / worked

sentence.da: Den gamle cykel vil ikke **duge** til så lang en tur.
sentence.en: The old bike will not do for such a long trip.

at dukke op.explanation: "At dukke op" means "to show up", often when someone arrives or something appears unexpectedly. On a screen it means "to pop up": "En besked dukker op" (A message pops up).

sentence.da: Jeg håber, at han vil **dukke op** i aften.
sentence.en: I hope that he will show up tonight.

at dumpe.explanation: "At dumpe" means "to fail (an exam)": "Han dumpede til eksamen" (He failed the exam). The opposite is "at bestå" (to pass): "Hun bestod eksamen" (She passed the exam).

sentence.da: Jeg vil ikke **dumpe** til eksamen.
sentence.en: I don't want to fail the exam.

at dykke.explanation: "At dykke" means "to dive" under water. To dive in headfirst from a board, say "at stupe" (to dive in): "Han stuper fra vippen" (He dives from the board).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne **dykke** og se fiskene i havet.
sentence.en: I would like to dive and see the fish in the sea.

at dyppe.explanation: "At dyppe" means "to dip", to put something briefly into a liquid or a sauce and take it out again. The dip is short, unlike "at lægge i blød" (to soak), where the thing stays in for a long time.

sentence.da: Børnene elsker at **dyppe** pommes frites i ketchup.
sentence.en: The children love to dip french fries in ketchup.

at dyrke.explanation: "At dyrke" means "to grow" plants on purpose: "Vi dyrker tomater" (We grow tomatoes). It also means "to practice" a sport or hobby: "Jeg dyrker yoga" (I do yoga).

sentence.da: Min mor vil **dyrke** grøntsager i haven.
sentence.en: My mother wants to grow vegetables in the garden.

at dyrke sport.explanation: "At dyrke sport" means "to do sports" as a regular activity. For one named sport, Danes often use "at spille" (to play): "Jeg spiller tennis" (I play tennis).

sentence.da: Jeg vil **dyrke sport** mere i år.
sentence.en: I want to do more sports this year.

at dække.explanation: "At dække" means "to cover", to put something over something else. It also means to pay for a cost or a loss: "Forsikringen dækker skaden" (The insurance covers the damage).

sentence.da: Jeg vil **dække** barnet med et tæppe.
sentence.en: I want to cover the child with a blanket.

at dække bord.explanation: "At dække bord" means "to set the table", putting out plates and cutlery before a meal: "Kan du dække bord til aftensmad?" (Can you set the table for dinner?)

sentence.da: Jeg skal **dække bord** til fem personer.
sentence.en: I have to set the table for five people.

at dække over.explanation: "At dække over" means "to cover up", to keep a mistake or a crime from coming out. With a person, it means to protect them by staying quiet about what they did: "Hun dækkede over sin bror" (She covered for her brother).

sentence.da: Han ville **dække over** fejlen, men sandheden kom frem.
sentence.en: He wanted to cover up the mistake, but the truth came out.

at dæmpe.explanation: "At dæmpe" means "to dampen", to make a sound, a light or a feeling weaker. To tell a person to calm down, say "Dæmp dig!" (Tone it down!)

sentence.da: Du må gerne **dæmpe** musikken, når naboerne sover.
sentence.en: You may turn the music down when the neighbors are asleep.

at dø.explanation: "At dø" means "to die". To say someone has died, Danish uses "er" (is) instead of "har" (has): "Han er død" (He has died; literally, "He is dead").

sentence.da: Planter kan **dø** uden vand.
sentence.en: Plants can die without water.

at døbe.explanation: "At døbe" means "to baptize", to welcome a person into the Christian church with water: "Hun blev døbt Maria" (She was baptized Maria). It is also used for giving a name to something: "Vi døbte hunden Bølle" (We named the dog Bølle).

sentence.da: Præsten skal **døbe** barnet på søndag.
sentence.en: The priest will baptize the child on Sunday.

at dømme.explanation: "At dømme" means "to judge" and "to sentence". In a court, it means to find someone guilty and set the punishment. Outside court, it is about forming an opinion of someone: "Man skal ikke dømme folk på udseendet" (You should not judge people by their looks).

sentence.da: Retten kan **dømme** ham til to års fængsel.
sentence.en: The court can sentence him to two years in prison.

da.explanation: "Da" means "when", for something that happened once in the past. For something that happens every time or has not happened yet, use "når" (when) instead: "Når jeg kommer hjem, laver jeg mad" (When I get home, I cook).

sentence.da: **Da** jeg kom hjem, sov børnene.
sentence.en: When I came home, the children were asleep.

dagen efter.explanation: "Dagen efter" means "the day after". Name the earlier event after it: "dagen efter festen" (the day after the party). Without an event, say "næste dag" (next day): "Næste dag tog vi hjem" (The next day we went home).

forms.en: The day after, he came home

sentence.da: Jeg var træt **dagen efter** festen.
sentence.en: I was tired the day after the party.

dagens ret.explanation: "Dagens ret" means "dish of the day". Word for word, it is the day's dish: dagens (the day's) and ret (dish).

sentence.da: **Dagens ret** er fisk og kartofler.
sentence.en: The dish of the day is fish and potatoes.

dagevis.explanation: "Dagevis" means "for days", one after another over a long stretch. The ending "-vis" marks a long stretch, as in "timevis" (for hours) and "ugevis" (for weeks).

sentence.da: Efter stormen var der **dagevis** uden strøm.
sentence.en: After the storm there was no power for days.

daglig.explanation: "Daglig" means "daily" and goes before the thing that happens every day: "en daglig avis" (a daily newspaper). To say how often you do something, use "hver dag" (every day): "Jeg løber hver dag" (I run every day).

sentence.da: Jeg tager en **daglig** gåtur.
sentence.en: I take a daily walk.

dagligdags.explanation: "Dagligdags" means "everyday" and describes ordinary things that happen all the time. It also describes language: "dagligdags sprog" (everyday language).

sentence.da: Indkøb og madlavning er **dagligdags** ting.
sentence.en: Shopping and cooking are everyday things.

dagligt.explanation: "Dagligt" means "daily" or "every day" and goes after the verb: "Jeg læser dagligt" (I read every day). In front of a thing, use "daglig" with "en" and "dagligt" with "et": "en daglig tur" (a daily walk), "et dagligt møde" (a daily meeting).

sentence.da: Han træner **dagligt** og spiser sundt.
sentence.en: He trains daily and eats healthily.

dagligvarer.explanation: "Dagligvarer" means "groceries": everyday goods like food and household things such as soap. A shop that sells them is "en dagligvarebutik" (a grocery store).

sentence.da: Jeg køber **dagligvarer** i supermarkedet.
sentence.en: I buy groceries at the supermarket.

dagpenge.explanation: "Dagpenge" means "unemployment benefits", money you get each day when you are out of work. You only get them if you are a member of an "a-kasse" (an unemployment insurance fund). Literally, the word means "day money".

sentence.da: Når man bliver fyret, kan man få **dagpenge** i en periode.
sentence.en: When you get fired, you can get unemployment benefits for a period.

dagslys.explanation: "Dagslys" means "daylight", the natural light you have while the sun is up, even on a cloudy day. Light from a lamp is not "dagslys".

sentence.da: Om vinteren er der kun få timer med **dagslys**.
sentence.en: In winter there are only a few hours of daylight.

damp.explanation: "Damp" means "steam", the hot cloud from boiling water. It is also what makes mirrors and windows misty.

forms.en: There is steam in the bathroom.

sentence.da: Når vand koger, bliver det til **damp**.
sentence.en: When water boils, it turns into steam.

dansk.explanation: "Dansk" means "Danish", the language and also things from Denmark: "dansk ost" (Danish cheese). As a school subject, it is used without an article: "Jeg har dansk" (I have Danish class). Language names start with a lowercase letter: "dansk" (Danish), "engelsk" (English).

sentence.da: Jeg bor i Danmark og taler **dansk**.
sentence.en: I live in Denmark and speak Danish.

data.explanation: "Data" means "data", facts and numbers collected for a purpose, for example in research or on a computer.

sentence.da: Vi bruger **data** fra mange mennesker.
sentence.en: We use data from many people.

datalogi.explanation: "Datalogi" means "computer science", the science of how data is stored and processed and how programs are made. It is the name of the university subject.

sentence.da: Hun læser **datalogi** og lærer at skrive programmer.
sentence.en: She studies computer science and learns to write programs.

datid.explanation: "En datid" means "past tense", the form of a word that tells you something has already happened. For the past as a period of history, say "fortid" (the past).

forms.da: datiden af at gå er gik
forms.en: the past tense of at gå is gik

sentence.da: Ordet spiste står i **datid**, fordi det allerede er sket.
sentence.en: The word spiste is in the past tense because it has already happened.

davs.explanation: "Davs" means "hi", a short, casual greeting for friends and people you know well. With someone you have just met, say "hej" (hi): "Hej, jeg hedder Anna" (Hi, my name is Anna).

sentence.da: **Davs**, Peter! Hvordan går det?
sentence.en: Hi, Peter! How is it going?

de.explanation: "De" means "they". To say they do something, use "de": "De ser mig" (They see me). To say you do something to them, use "dem" (them): "Jeg ser dem" (I see them). "De" is also "the" before more than one thing when a word like "store" (big) comes first: "de store huse" (the big houses).

sentence.da: Anna og Lars? **De** er hjemme.
sentence.en: Anna and Lars? They are at home.

december.explanation: "December" means "December". Danish writes month names with a lowercase letter, so you write "i december" (in December), not "i December".

sentence.da: Vi fejrer jul i **december**.
sentence.en: We celebrate Christmas in December.

dedikeret.explanation: "Dedikeret" means "dedicated", for a person who gives a lot of time and effort to a job or cause. It can also mean made for one use only: "en dedikeret server" (a dedicated server).

sentence.da: Hun er en **dedikeret** lærer og bruger mange timer på sine elever.
sentence.en: She is a dedicated teacher and spends many hours on her pupils.

defekt.explanation: "Defekt" means "defective", for a machine or part that does not work as it should. It sounds technical, as on a repair form. In everyday talk, say "ødelagt" (broken): "Min telefon er ødelagt" (My phone is broken).

sentence.da: Vaskemaskinen er **defekt**, og den vil ikke starte.
sentence.en: The washing machine is defective, and it will not start.

dejlig.explanation: "Dejlig" means "lovely" or "nice", for things you enjoy, such as "dejligt vejr" (lovely weather) and "en dejlig dag" (a lovely day).

sentence.da: Det er en **dejlig** varm sommerdag.
sentence.en: It is a lovely warm summer day.

dels ... dels.explanation: "Dels ... dels" means "partly ... partly", for listing two reasons or sides that each matter. At the start of a sentence, the verb comes right after the first "dels" (partly): "Dels er det dyrt, dels er det svært" (Partly it is expensive, partly it is hard).

forms.da: dels for sjov, dels for pengene
forms.en: partly for fun, partly for the money
partly at home, partly at the office

related.da: på den ene side ... på den anden side
related.en: on the one hand ... on the other

sentence.da: Hvorfor jeg bor her? **Dels ... dels**: jobbet og familien.
sentence.en: Why do I live here? Partly ... partly: the job and the family.

deltagelse.explanation: "Deltagelse" means "participation", being involved in an event, a class or a project. It is followed by "i" (in): "deltagelse i kurset" (participation in the course).

sentence.da: Din **deltagelse** i mødet er vigtig for os.
sentence.en: Your participation in the meeting is important to us.

dem.explanation: "Dem" means "them". To say something is done to them, use "dem": "Jeg ser dem" (I see them). To say they do something, use "de" (they): "De ser mig" (They see me).

sentence.da: Mine naboer er søde. Jeg kender **dem**.
sentence.en: My neighbors are nice. I know them.

demokratisk.explanation: "Demokratisk" means "democratic", for a country, group or decision where the people decide, usually by voting.

sentence.da: I et **demokratisk** land vælger folket selv sine politikere.
sentence.en: In a democratic country, the people choose their own politicians.

den.explanation: "Den" means "it" for words that take "en": "Jeg har en bil. Den er rød" (I have a car. It is red). For words that take "et", use "det" (it): "Jeg har et hus. Det er rødt" (I have a house. It is red). "Den" also means "the" before a describing word: "den røde bil" (the red car).

sentence.da: Se på bilen! **Den** er meget stor.
sentence.en: Look at the car! It is very big.

den offentlige sektor.explanation: "Den offentlige sektor" means "the public sector", all the work paid for by taxes: offices, hospitals, schools and local councils. The part run by companies is "den private sektor" (the private sector).

forms.da: at arbejde i den offentlige sektor
forms.en: to work in the public sector

sentence.da: Lærere og sygeplejersker arbejder i **den offentlige sektor**.
sentence.en: Teachers and nurses work in the public sector.

den tid, den sorg.explanation: "Den tid, den sorg" means "cross that bridge when we come to it": do not stress about a problem before it actually happens. Word for word, it means "that time, that sorrow".

forms.en: We'll cross that bridge when we come to it

forms.da: Det tager vi, når det sker
forms.en: We'll deal with that when it happens

forms.da: Hvad hvis det går galt? Den tid, den sorg
forms.en: What if it goes wrong? We'll cross that bridge when we come to it

sentence.da: Måske bliver det dyrt senere, men **den tid, den sorg**.
sentence.en: Maybe it will get expensive later, but we'll cross that bridge when we come to it.

dengang.explanation: "Dengang" means "back then" and always points to the past. It is built from den (that) and gang (time), so it literally means "that time".

forms.en: What were you doing back then?
My father lived here back then.

sentence.da: **Dengang** boede vi i Odense og var glade.
sentence.en: Back then we lived in Odense and were happy.

denim.explanation: "Denim" means "denim", the strong, usually blue cloth that jeans are made of.

sentence.da: Jakken er af **denim**, og den holder i mange år.
sentence.en: The jacket is made of denim, and it lasts for many years.

denne.explanation: "Denne" means "this" with words that take "en": "denne bil" (this car). For words that take "et", use "dette" (this): "dette hus" (this house). "Denne" sounds formal; in everyday speech people say "den her bil" (this car).

sentence.da: Jeg vil have **denne** bil.
sentence.en: I want this car.

dens.explanation: "Dens" means "its", for something you say with "en", like "en bil" (a car) or "en stol" (a chair). For something you say with "et", use "dets" (its): "Huset er gammelt, men dets tag er nyt" (The house is old, but its roof is new).

sentence.da: Bilen er gammel, men **dens** motor er stærk.
sentence.en: The car is old, but its engine is strong.

deprimerende.explanation: "Deprimerende" means "depressing", something that pulls your mood down. It names what causes the feeling: "en deprimerende film" (a depressing movie). How you feel is "deprimeret" (depressed): "Jeg er deprimeret" (I am depressed).

sentence.da: Regnen og mørket om vinteren kan være **deprimerende**.
sentence.en: The rain and darkness in winter can be depressing.

deprimeret.explanation: "Deprimeret" means "depressed", feeling very low and without energy or hope: "Hun har været deprimeret i flere måneder" (She has been depressed for months). What causes the feeling is "deprimerende" (depressing): "en deprimerende film" (a depressing movie).

sentence.da: Han føler sig **deprimeret** og har ikke lyst til at se nogen.
sentence.en: He feels depressed and does not want to see anyone.

der.explanation: "Der" means "there": "Han er der" (He is there). Use "her" (here) for the place you are: "Han er her" (He is here). At the start of a sentence, "der" says something exists: "Der er mange børn" (There are many children). It can also mean "who": "manden, der bor her" (the man who lives here).

sentence.da: **Der** er en kat i haven.
sentence.en: There is a cat in the garden.

der er ingen ko på isen.explanation: "Der er ingen ko på isen" means "there's nothing to worry about": the danger is over or never existed. Word for word, it says there is no cow on the ice. The opposite is "Der er ko på isen" (There is trouble).

forms.da: Der er ingen ko på isen
forms.en: There is nothing to worry about

forms.da: Rolig, der er ingen ko på isen
Der er ingen ko på isen, vi har god tid
forms.en: There's nothing to worry about, we have plenty of time

sentence.da: Alt er klaret, og **der er ingen ko på isen**.
sentence.en: Everything is taken care of, and there is nothing to worry about.

derefter.explanation: "Derefter" means "after that": "Jeg spiste, og derefter gik jeg" (I ate, and after that I left). To name the earlier event, use "efter" (after) in front of it: "efter maden" (after the meal).

sentence.da: Først mad, og **derefter** kaffe.
sentence.en: First food, and after that coffee.

deres.explanation: "Deres" means "their": "Det er deres hus" (It is their house). Write "deres" the same way before one thing or several: "deres hund" (their dog), "deres hunde" (their dogs).

sentence.da: Anna og Bo bor i **deres** hus.
sentence.en: Anna and Bo live in their house.

derfor.explanation: "Derfor" means "that is why". The same fact can be said two ways: "Jeg er syg, derfor bliver jeg hjemme" (I am sick, that is why I am staying home) and "Jeg bliver hjemme, fordi jeg er syg" (I am staying home because I am sick).

forms.en: that is why I am here

sentence.da: Det regner. **Derfor** er jeg hjemme.
sentence.en: It is raining. That is why I am home.

derfra.explanation: "Derfra" means "from there" and tells where something comes from, a place away from you: "Jeg kommer derfra" (I come from there). For your own place, use "herfra" (from here): "Jeg kommer herfra" (I come from here).

forms.en: What can you see from there?

sentence.da: Aarhus er flot. Min mor kommer **derfra**.
sentence.en: Aarhus is beautiful. My mother comes from there.

derhen.explanation: "Derhen" means "(to) there" and is used when you move toward a place. To name the place where a person stays, use "der" (there): "Han er der" (He is there).

sentence.da: Skal vi gå **derhen** sammen?
sentence.en: Shall we walk there together?

derhjemme.explanation: "Derhjemme" means "at home", used when you talk about your own home from somewhere else: "Hvad spiser I derhjemme?" (What do you eat at home?). Do not mix it up with "hjemme" (at home), which says where you are right now: "Jeg er hjemme" (I am at home).

forms.en: what do you do at home?

sentence.da: **Derhjemme** spiser vi sent.
sentence.en: At home we eat late.

derimod.explanation: "Derimod" means "on the other hand", showing a contrast with what was just said: "Min bror er høj. Jeg er derimod lav." (My brother is tall. I, on the other hand, am short.) Put it right after the verb.

forms.da: Prisen er høj. Kvaliteten derimod er god.
forms.en: The price is high. The quality, on the other hand, is good.
You, on the other hand, are right

sentence.da: Byen er larmende. Landet er **derimod** stille.
sentence.en: The city is noisy. The countryside, on the other hand, is quiet.

derinde.explanation: "Derinde" means "in there" and points to a place inside something, away from you, such as another room: "Katten er derinde" (The cat is in there). For your own place, use "herinde" (in here): "Jeg er herinde" (I am in here).

forms.en: in there in the living room

sentence.da: Min mor er **derinde** i stuen.
sentence.en: My mother is in there in the living room.

dermed.explanation: "Dermed" means "thereby" and "with that". Use it to say what follows from what you just did: "Han skrev under, og dermed er aftalen indgået" (He signed, and thereby the deal is made). It is built from der (there) and med (with).

sentence.da: Vi har betalt, og **dermed** er sagen afgjort.
sentence.en: We have paid, and with that the matter is settled.

dernede.explanation: "Dernede" means "down there" and points to a place lower than you, away from you, such as a basement or the floor below: "Katten er dernede" (The cat is down there). For a place higher than you, use "deroppe" (up there): "Katten er deroppe" (The cat is up there).

sentence.da: Bilen står **dernede** i kælderen.
sentence.en: The car is down there in the basement.

dernæst.explanation: "Dernæst" means "next" and "then", for the next step in a series. In a speech or a list you say it after "først" (first): "Først kommer maden, dernæst kommer kaffen" (First comes the food, next comes the coffee).

sentence.da: Først skærer du løget, og **dernæst** steger du det i smør.
sentence.en: First you cut the onion, and then you fry it in butter.

deroppe.explanation: "Deroppe" means "up there" and tells where something is when it is higher than you and away from you. It is built from der (there) and oppe (up).

forms.en: The cat is sitting up there

sentence.da: Kan du se fuglen **deroppe** i træet?
sentence.en: Can you see the bird up there in the tree?

derovre.explanation: "Derovre" means "over there", for a place at a distance that you can point to: "Bogen ligger derovre" (The book is over there). To move there, use "derover" (over there, with movement): "Jeg går derover" (I am going over there).

sentence.da: Min bil står **derovre** ved huset.
sentence.en: My car is parked over there by the house.

derude.explanation: "Derude" means "out there" and points to a place outside or farther out, away from you: "Børnene er derude" (The children are out there). For inside something, use "derinde" (in there): "Børnene er derinde" (The children are in there).

sentence.da: Se ud af vinduet! Børnene leger **derude**.
sentence.en: Look out of the window! The children are playing out there.

derudover.explanation: "Derudover" means "in addition", adding one more point to what you just said. At the start of a sentence, the verb follows right after it: "Derudover har vi en have" (In addition, we have a garden).

forms.en: In addition, we have a garden

sentence.da: Han arbejder på kontoret, og **derudover** passer han en lille butik.
sentence.en: He works at an office, and in addition he runs a small shop.

design.explanation: "Design" means "design", how something is planned to look and work, like a chair, a phone or a website. It is also a job field: "Hun arbejder med design" (She works in design).

sentence.da: Jeg kan lide stolens **design** og farve.
sentence.en: I like the chair's design and color.

desperat.explanation: "Desperat" means "desperate", for a person who sees no way out or for what the person does. To name what you are desperate to get, use "efter" (for): "Hun er desperat efter et job" (She is desperate for a job).

sentence.da: Han var **desperat** og ringede til alle.
sentence.en: He was desperate and called everyone.

desto.explanation: "Desto" means "the" in a pair like "the more..., the better". It comes in the second half, after "jo" (the) in the first: "Jo mere du øver, desto bedre bliver du" (The more you practice, the better you get).

sentence.da: Jo ældre vinen er, **desto** dyrere bliver den.
sentence.en: The older the wine is, the more expensive it gets.

desuden.explanation: "Desuden" means "furthermore" and "besides". Use it to add one more point, often a final reason: "Huset er for dyrt. Desuden ligger det langt væk." (The house is too expensive. Besides, it is far away.)

sentence.da: Jeg er træt, og **desuden** er det sent.
sentence.en: I am tired, and besides, it is late.

desværre.explanation: "Desværre" means "unfortunately". Use it before bad news or a no. It sounds softer and more polite than just "Nej" (No).

sentence.da: **Desværre** har jeg ikke tid i dag.
sentence.en: Unfortunately, I do not have time today.

det.explanation: "Det" means "it" or "that". Use it for a thing that takes "et": "Jeg har et hus, og det er stort" (I have a house, and it is big). Things that take "en" use "den": "Jeg har en bil, og den er stor" (I have a car, and it is big). "Det" is also used when there is no particular thing, such as weather and comments: "Det regner" (It is raining), "Det er sjovt" (That is fun).

forms.en: I know it / I know that.

sentence.da: Se på huset! **Det** er meget gammelt.
sentence.en: Look at the house! It is very old.

det er.explanation: "Det er" means "it is" or "that is"; Danish uses the same two words for both. Use it to name things or describe them: "Det er en bog" (It is a book).

sentence.da: **Det er** en god dag i dag.
sentence.en: It is a good day today.

det er en god idé.explanation: "Det er en god idé" means "that's a good idea", said to agree with a suggestion. You can shorten it to "God idé!" (Good idea!).

sentence.da: Café i dag? **Det er en god idé.**
sentence.en: Cafe today? That's a good idea.

det er fint med mig.explanation: "Det er fint med mig" means "that's fine with me" and agrees to a plan. Change "mig" (me) to "dig" (you) to ask: "Er det fint med dig?" (Is that fine with you?).

forms.da: Ja, det er fint med mig.
Hvis det er fint med dig.

sentence.da: Vi ses klokken fem? **Det er fint med mig.**
sentence.en: See you at five? That's fine with me.

det er hip som hap.explanation: "Det er hip som hap" means "it's six of one, half a dozen of the other": two choices are equally good. Say it when you are asked to choose and you do not mind: "Kaffe eller te? Det er hip som hap" (Coffee or tea? Either is fine).

forms.da: Det er hip som hap, hvad vi vælger
forms.en: It's all the same what we choose

forms.da: Det er hip som hap, om vi går nu eller senere
forms.en: It makes no difference whether we go now or later

sentence.da: **Det er hip som hap**, fordi bussen og toget koster det samme.
sentence.en: It's all the same, because the bus and the train cost the same.

det er i orden.explanation: "Det er i orden" means "it's okay" or "that's fine". Danes say it in reply to "undskyld" (sorry) and to agree to a plan. "I orden" literally means "in order".

sentence.da: Undskyld! — **Det er i orden.**
sentence.en: Sorry! — It's okay.

det er ikke så svært.explanation: "Det er ikke så svært" means "it's not that hard", something you say to reassure someone about a task. "Svært" means "difficult" and "ikke så" means "not so".

sentence.da: Dansk? **Det er ikke så svært.**
sentence.en: Danish? It's not that hard.

det er lige det.explanation: "Det er lige det" means "that's exactly it" and you say it when someone has hit the right point. Said short, "lige det" means "exactly that": "Jeg ville have lige det" (I wanted exactly that).

forms.da: Det er lige det, jeg mener
Nej, det er ikke lige det

sentence.da: Præcis, **det er lige det**, jeg mener.
sentence.en: Exactly, that's just what I mean.

det er lige meget.explanation: "Det er lige meget" means "it doesn't matter". Say it when you do not mind which option is chosen. "Det er mig lige meget" (I don't care) can sound rude.

forms.da: Det er lige meget, hvad du vælger.
forms.en: It doesn't matter what you choose.

sentence.da: Te eller kaffe? **Det er lige meget.**
sentence.en: Tea or coffee? It doesn't matter.

det er min skyld.explanation: "Det er min skyld" means "it's my fault" and takes the blame. Change "min" (my) to "hans" (his) to blame someone else: "Det er hans skyld" (It's his fault).

sentence.da: Jeg glemte at ringe, **det er min skyld**.
sentence.en: I forgot to call, it's my fault.

det er rigtigt.explanation: "Det er rigtigt" means "that's right", said to agree that something is correct or true. Do not mix it up with "rigtig" used as "really" before another word, as in "rigtig godt" (really good). A short alternative is "ja, præcis" (yes, exactly).

sentence.da: Du bor i Aarhus? **Det er rigtigt.**
sentence.en: You live in Aarhus? That's right.

det er synd.explanation: "Det er synd" means "that's a shame" or "that's too bad", and you say it when something bad happens to someone. To name the person you feel sorry for, add "for" (for): "Det er synd for dig" (That's too bad for you).

sentence.da: Du kan ikke komme? **Det er synd!**
sentence.en: You can't come? That's a shame!
